cards.title: Owed a billion dollars in Nvidia stock

depth.text: an early **NVIDIA** adviser says a **stock-option mix-up** left him short millions of shares

His 1993 agreement said all **25,000 options** would vest after one year. He says stock splits turned the missing 9,375 into **4.5 million shares**, but he and his lawyers concluded the **statute of limitations** was against them.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say the options expired and the claim is dead; others suggest suing over the information he received or selling the right to litigate.

comments.text: You are ultimately responsible for asserting your contractual rights. Your stock options had an expiry and you did not exercise them in time. The letter you received notifying that you had 15,625 vested options was not an award in of itself, it was only a courtesy notifying you that you had vested options to exercise before they expired. Even if due to ambiguous wording it could be argued that…

You should sell your right to litigate this. There are hundreds of firms that would pay you to take this on. Would involve near zero effort for you and would also check the box of being “about the principle”.

An open question is what happened to the 15,625 shares that he received when he exercised his options in 1996? If he had held on to those, they would be worth even more than the additional 9,375 shares he was entitled to -- about $1.7 billion using the same numbers in the post. My guess is that he probably sold them when they were worth a lot less then they are now, and would have done the same…

Author here. Thanks for all the comments, I've been hesitant to post this to the court of public opinion, yet curiosity about what the HN community would think caused me to push the button. My lawyers - who were really excellent - represented me (on contingency!) because it seemed the chance of a judge not accepting a motion to dismiss (for a variety of reasons I don't want to detail here) was…

> Here in the land of the free, it turns out a company only has to honor its contractual obligations for a little while. If Nvidia showed you contract paperwork that proved they overpaid you 9,375 shares in 1993, would you agree to pay them back the present value? After all contracts should be enforceable indefinitely right?

cards.title: Show HN: Lofi Cities – Pixel-art city nights with browser-generated lofi

depth.text: someone made **pixel-art city nights** with **lofi music** generated live in your browser
Each scene is a **480×270 pixel animation** that loops **every four minutes**, with its own weather and city sounds. Tracks are **synthesized live in the browser**, with no samples or recordings.

cards.camps: Two camps: fans call it gorgeous and cool; critics say it feels too AI-generated and the ads break the immersion.

comments.text: The product hunt ad is breaking the immersion for me. I know that most cities have ads but still, I prefer ad free pixel art. It’s also not realistic, in one landscape the billboard is taller than a 9 story building.
I still love Mark Ferrari’s Living Worlds from 1995 which changes with the time of day & the month. Handmade and ad-free of course. https://www.effectgames.com/demos/worlds/

There's a lot to like here, but too AI-generated for me. The pixel art for Tokyo & Hong Kong don't use proper Chinese/Japanese characters. The pulsating badges in the non-pixel UI are also pretty AI-indicative in a way that is distracting.
I don't why I would want to stare at vibecoded UI and an ad to relax

Gorgeous, very well executed. I'm guessing the primary request will be more cities but I'll deviate and say I'd love to see more views as well. Would be nice to have the same set of cities by I can see it from a studio view same way it is in the Paris view. Or from an office. Or a cafe.

cards.title: Don't couple your Go code to GitHub

depth.text: someone says Go packages should use **custom domains** so changing code hosts won't mean rewriting **import paths**

Go uses the hosting location in an **import path**, so moving hosts can mean changing code. The author recommends a custom domain that can point somewhere new while users keep the **same install command**. One company used GitHub, GitLab and Azure Devops at once because switching was such a large task, and ended up paying for **three hosting services**.

cards.camps: Two camps: custom-domain advocates say they avoid tying package names to one host; critics say domains need upkeep and can disappear, while some say a go.mod replace or find-and-replace is enough.

comments.text: True, but beware of the domain name you're using. Because VeriSign may unilaterally decide to delete your domain name along with thousands of others [1] and you're back to square one… [1] https://neil.fraser.name/news/2026/09/03/

> In my opinion, every commerical software development team using Go should be using custom domains for namespacing their internal libraries and packages. I’d remove “go” from the above, i.e. I think same applies to other stacks. Even using GitHub domain links in code comments gets problematic long term. Ie when a migration happens and those links start pointing nowhere.

> That is, if you move your git hosting to GitLab then you have to change your code! You can also just use "replace github.com/example/example => gitlab.com/example/example" in your go.mod file and everything will keep working. That seems like a very pre-mature optimization for something that doesn't really matter.

> One of the good features of Go is that you namespace your code with the location to fetch the code. Then the rest of the article explains why this is NOT a good feature in practice. I don't think it's unworkable either, but this is one of these little thing that Go decided to do different and convinced its fans that this is a great idea and all the other languages where doing it wrong. After a…

Great when a company goes out of business and the domains are dangling. Next one to scoop it up takes over source code that others new depend on. We've seen this many times already in other ecosystems. It is a very bad situation. It is bad advice to move your packages under your own domain. You will never be as good as Microsoft to keep paying for the domain. There are no guarantees in life but I…

cards.title: PostmarketOS is rebranding as Nura

depth.text: the **postmarketOS project** is now called **Nura**, a shorter name picked after a long search

The team says the old name was **hard to pronounce and remember**, and its descriptive wording no longer fit the project’s scope. **Nura** is an abbreviation of Nuraghe, ancient granite structures in Sardinia; Davide Depau suggested the name. The team picked it using **range voting** after a selection team narrowed 300+ community suggestions to four names.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say Nura is catchier and rolls off the tongue; others say postmarketOS explained the project better and Nura sounds generic.

comments.text: Have you seen the new show? It's on Tubu. It's literally on Heebee. It's on Poodee with ads. It's literally on Dippy. You can probably find it on Weeno. Dude it's on Gumpy. It's a Pheebo original. It's on Poob. You can watch it on Poob. You can go to Poob and watch it. Log onto Poob right now. Go to Poob. Dive into Poob. You can Poob it. It's on Poob. Poob has it for you. Poob has it for you.

Idk, I think the new name sounds too corporate, like some shitty startup or wellness brand. PostmarketOS was a bit of a mouthful but it gave you some idea of what the project was. Well, if they think it's a way to reach more people, then more power to them.

I did think postmarketOS was a bit of an awkward name but it was also widely recognised, at least in Linux nerd circles. I guess this will cause a bit of confusion in the short term but hopefully lead to broader recognition in the longer term. Though the obstacles to Nura's growth are probably not primarily branding-related.

Searching for "Nura" returns dozens of existing results. They couldn't even get nura.org! Is there really not a more distinct name they could've picked? Even Nura OS would make them easier to find in the long term. Non-exhaustive list of things already named "nura": - NURA: Premium Ingredients for Food & Wellness - Nura - Award-winning personalised sound - NURA: India's First Ai Powered Health…
I'm torn; the old name was awkward, but renaming is a painful breaking change. Oh well, it's done now.

cards.title: Replacing the old battery on rechargeable bike lights

depth.text: someone got **old rechargeable bike lights** working again by **replacing their batteries** at a makerspace
They soldered in replacement batteries after an LLM suggested the old one was an **LIR2477**. The lights work, but the writer hasn’t tested how long the new batteries last yet.

cards.camps: Two camps: one says decode the battery code and measure the cell; another says matching chemistry, voltage, and capacity matters more than the exact model.

comments.text: > I wasn’t sure how to find out what an “LI????77” was […]. I would be interested to learn non-LLM ways to figure this out though. There must be a way. Reading https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Button_cell#Type_designation would have indicated a solution: The third character must be an R (for rechargeable), the “77” would be the height in tenths of millimeters (which makes for a good plausibility…

> I wasn’t sure how to find out what an “LI????77” was […]. I would be interested to learn non-LLM ways to figure this out though. There must be a way. Back in my days I simply googled my way through the nomenclature of batteries. I feel pretty old, somehow.

Love this. I have a pile of nice Cygolites (both front and tail) that my whole family uses that are maybe 8 or 9 years old. Their capacities have largely dropped to the point that I need to charge them every ride or two. Maybe get about 90 minutes of use, down from 3-4 hours previously. They're not user-serviceable by design but I've been pondering cracking them open and having a go at swapping…

I wouldn't worry about matching the exact model number of the battery. Instead, it's more important to get roughly the same chemistry and a capacity equal or maybe a touch greater (if technology improved in the last 10 years, capacity could be greater with modern parts). Specific batteries go in and out of production. But as long as it's the same CHEMISTRY, voltage, and capacity, it's likely…

Word of warning: batteries from AliExpress might not be the size it says on the tin. Also: not all lights require soldering to change the battery. Some brands, like Fenix, offer lights where you can change the battery on the go. I had a light from a lesser known Taiwanese brand - an INFINI Lava 500.
At some point it stopped working, so I took it apart with my iFixit kit and inside was a 102660…

glossary.stock options: A deal that gives someone the right to buy company shares later at an agreed price.
glossary.vest: When options vest, the holder earns the right to buy the shares under the deal.
glossary.stock split: A company divides each share into more shares, with each one representing a smaller part of the company.
glossary.statute of limitations: A legal deadline for starting a case about something that happened.
glossary.motion to dismiss: A request asking a judge to end a case before it goes to trial.
glossary.pixel art: Pictures built from visible colored squares, often with a blocky look.
glossary.Web Audio API: A set of tools built into browsers for making and controlling sound.
glossary.sound synthesis: Making sounds electronically instead of playing recorded audio.
glossary.import path: The address Go uses to identify and fetch a package.
glossary.Go vanity URL: A custom web address that lets a Go package keep the same name even if its code host changes.
glossary.go.mod: A project file that tells Go which other packages it depends on.
glossary.301 redirect: A web instruction that permanently sends someone from one address to another.
glossary.operating system: The main software that runs a device and lets other programs work on it.
glossary.range voting: A way to choose by letting each voter give options scores, then comparing those scores.
glossary.trademark: A name or logo legally protected so people can tell whose product or project it is.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.soldering: Joining electronic parts by melting a little metal onto their connections.
glossary.desoldering pump: A hand tool that sucks melted solder off a connection so a part can come loose.
glossary.LIR2477: A battery code; commenters say the R marks a rechargeable cell and 77 gives its height in tenths of a millimetre.
glossary.battery chemistry: The kind of materials inside a battery, which affects how it works and what charger it needs.
glossary.voltage: A measure of the electrical push a battery provides.
glossary.capacity: How much energy a battery can store, which affects how long it can run something.
